fatal_errors: The proposed Nb–Mo–Ta–W substrate and Zr-based metallic-glass coating do not reconstruct the target HfZrTi(TaNbV)x alloying intervention.
The claim that uncoated Nb–Mo–Ta–W has impact-induced energy-release behavior is unsupported; the cited evidence does not establish reactive fragmentation or oxidation-based energy release.
Neither citation supports depositing a 2–5 μm Zr-based metallic-glass coating on bulk Nb–Mo–Ta–W, its adhesion under impact, or crack-arrest-mediated tensile ductility.
The hypothesis omits the target phase-control mechanism involving Ta/Nb/V stabilization of BCC, suppression of HCP/omega phases, and solid-solution strengthening.
The proposed energy-release measurement is undefined and does not reproduce the oxygen-dependent, approximately 4000 s^-1 fragmentation and luminosity test needed to assess energetic performance.
explanation: The response addresses the broad design objective and offers a controlled coated-versus-uncoated experiment with an explicit falsification rule, but it is scientifically disconnected from the target system. The target intervention is bulk alloying of as-cast HfZrTi with equimolar Ta–Nb–V, particularly x = 0.9, whereas the response substitutes a different alloy and an unsupported surface coating. E1 concerns fabrication of NbMoTaW films on ceramic substrates, not coating a bulk NbMoTaW energetic alloy with Zr-based metallic glass. E2 discusses plasticity and shear bands in an amorphous HEA film but does not establish the proposed coating composition, crack-arrest mechanism, interface performance, or preservation of impact-induced energy release. The experiment could test some coating claims, but it needs quantitative strain mapping, replicated strength and elongation criteria, and an air-versus-inert high-rate fragmentation/luminosity measurement to distinguish mechanical energy absorption from oxidation-based energy release.
